title: #76 Lars Stenlund on Driven by Curiosity
transcript:
Hello everyone and welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by RedEye.
I'm your host, Edie Palmen, and today we're thrilled to have Lars Stenlund on the show.
In 1985, Lars co-founded Vitek Software in Umeå, a city in northern Sweden, with 130,000
inhabitants.
Still, headquartered in Umeå, Vitek is today a large cap company listed at Nasdaq.com with
a market cap of about $1.5 billion.
Lars Stenlund was born in 1958 and was the CEO of Vitek for 35 years.
Since 2021, he's the chairman of the board and remains one of the largest shareholders
with 19% of the votes.
Celebrating Vitek's 40th anniversary in 2025, the company and author Patrick Suleian compiled
a book about a remarkable journey from a small venture at Umeå University to becoming
a leading company in vertical software solutions.
The summer, Lars and Vitek CEO, Ulebakma, were kind enough to give us a copy, and the
book's title is Driven by Curiosity.
We're excited to have one of its main contributors on the podcast today.
Here comes our conversation with Lars Stenlund.
Hi Lars and welcome to Investing by the Books podcast.
Thank you.
Thank you for having me.
It's great to have you here in RedEye Studio in Stockholm.
Thank you for taking the time.
Where do you normally live and work?
Usually say that I pay my taxes in Umeå, where I am, that's up for debate.
To begin, I'm curious, how did you grow up and how did I shape you?
Maybe you should ask my mother, she's still alive, and she has varied, very firm opinions
on stuff.
But I grew up in Schlefteo, which is about 130 kilometers north of Umeå.
I came to Umeå as a student, close to 50 years ago now.
But growing up, my father was working for the hydropower plant company, so I was brought
up within the energy sector or electricity sector, whatever.
But my grandparents were farmers, to various degrees.
My grandfather on my father's side was actually one of the first employees in Bouliden and
was making the drilling for prospecting in the late 20s or something, before the mine
actually opened.
And Bouliden is, as you know, still a well-known Swedish company.
Did you have any natural mentors during this time when you grew up?
For running a company, or whatever, in life?
Well, not really.
I had one experience or encounter the last year in the proper high school.
You know, we were on the study visit at an engineering firm.
And it was shown around and looked at different stuff.
And then we came into electronics laboratory.
And a guy was sitting there, a very old guy, probably in his 40s.
And we were curious, how did you decide to go into electronics?
And he said, well, I'm not really sure what I'm going to do in life, but this is pretty
interesting.
So I'm doing that in the meantime.
So making long-term plans for what I'm going to do, or what I'm going to become, so
forth, it felt a lot of weight, fell off my shoulders at that point in time.
And so you don't have to decide so much.
After military service and a summer job at a metal plant, he chose to study physics
in Umeå.
Yeah.
Why did you do that?
I wasn't prepared to go to work, so I wanted to find being a student for a while.
And since I still was interested in natural science, and it was fairly easy to get in that education
or that line of training.
So yeah, ended up in physics and mathematics.
And if you wouldn't have studied physics, what do you think you would have done in the
future?
Low, maybe.
Well, it was lucky that you did study physics, and eventually that made you co-found
a V-Tech, which we will speak about today, fittingly enough, the book driven by curiosity,
the first 40 years of V-Tech.
How did this book come about?
So it was people around, within the company, said, oh, we are coming up to 40 years.
And it's been on the table several times in the past also, if you shouldn't document
something about the company.
And as long as I was the acting CEO, I said, we don't have time.
But since I left four years ago, obviously we had time to make a book now at the 40 years
of anniversary.
So it's not my decision, but I have happily contributed.
Yeah.
And Patrick Surian is the one who has compiled the book and is the author.
Who is he?
Part of him is a sort of cultural geek, but he's also been the investor relations guy at
know it, Swedish consultancy company.
And he has his roots in Umeå also.
So he's qualified in every respect.
And what are the ambitions with the book?
Who is it for?
Well, it's mainly for our own people, for our own co-workers, to document history, of
course, and to maybe get inspiration that you don't need to know everything for the future.
You can be curious, and that's good enough.
A lot of times.
Yeah.
It's been a real pleasure to read the book, and it's quite extensive.
It's 260 pages, there's a lot of photos, a lot of documents.
I'm sure that many of our listeners would like to read the book, but I didn't find it online
to buy.
And as you said, it's for employees mainly.
Is it possible to get hold of it?
I think the only way to possibly get a hand on it is to contact our investor relations department.
And I know there are some discussions internally whether or not there should be a second edition
or not.
I'm not sure where that is at this point in time.
We'll see.
The title of the book is Driven by Curiosity.
Can you tell us a bit what this means to you?
I have said in the past that one of my absolute biggest achievements in life is that I spent
22 years in school and I came out still curious.
And there's a lot of stories on me as a kid being so curious that people just wanted me
to shut up.
I think that's one part of it.
The other part is 20 years or so ago, people started asking me and all of my co-founder,
what's your driving force guys?
And we looked at each other and said driving force and I don't know.
Like this is fun.
But we eventually came up with, we are both curious, probably.
That's probably our driving force.
So let's go back to the beginning of VTEC.
You mentioned all of how did it all start.
It started.
I was a PhD student and it was my tutor sort of.
So we had working together on a daily basis with my PhD project.
And halfway through my PhD studies, he tapped on my shoulders one day and we were having
lunch.
And he said, something like my friend or boy, I don't know how much you're.
You and I, we need to have a hobby.
I asked him what do you really mean having a hobby.
I'm working 24-7 with my thesis.
Yeah, I was sure, but we needed to have a hobby together.
But he has a, you know, a fork behind the ear.
So I reckon something was up.
So now he said like this, then I can get money for us to buy a personal computer.
This was in 1984, maybe, early 1984.
And you know software.
You can teach me how to code, making software.
And then you can have the PC every second week.
And there was okay, there was an idea that we could make computer software to support
real estate owners in Sweden to keep track of their energy consumption.
Because energy consumption and conservation was, in principle, my thesis.
So that was what I actually was doing.
And in order to be an experimentalist to which I was, you do, you make a lot of measurements.
And in order to make any sense of all those measurements, you need to compute.
And in those days, you needed to write all your software yourself.
So I was actually coding every, every hour of the day, in order to process my data.
But you said you had so much to do, you were working 24-7 with your thesis.
How come you still jumped on this opportunity?
Possibly because I'm curious.
That makes sense.
And how were those early days building the company?
We made, started out, trying to produce the software.
And we actually had some contacts within the property management consultants, businesses.
And they wanted to use our software in order to promote their consultancy services.
We made a deal with them to actually to sell it.
So we didn't meet any customers for the first five years.
I usually refer to the first five years as the dark ages because working with the company
was done during nights when the sun was out.
Yeah, and was there a monetary aspect?
Was that important at all to you at that time?
From one point of view, because every penny we made, we could buy new stuff for technical stuff.
Yeah.
First one computer, then two computers, and then some acoustic modems.
So we could communicate and then some more measurement stuff and so forth.
And software development kits and whatever.
Did it feel easy doing this or?
Well, that's I would put in the cabinet of interesting questions.
I can't tell.
I mean, that was just, I was 25, 26, 27 full steam ahead.
I don't know.
Did you ever consider giving up during those years or?
No, not really.
Now, I was eventually kind of fed up with the academic system.
So I was at the end of my PhD.
I got actually a tenure as an associate or a assistant professor.
I'm not sure what the teacher, teaching professor anyway, in electronics, which I appealed
for a couple of years in between before actually where I could draw a salary from the company.
You did make some success with the early ventures, the first business that you created with those
energy systems?
It was possible to sell it, yes.
But you also had quite some struggles during those times, when you start with nothing, virtually
nothing.
And so you have your funding has to be provided by what you can sell and no other means of funding.
So you have to prioritize harshly or very rigid, or whatever word you would like to use,
but I think you get the picture.
And as you got more and more successful, many entrepreneurs, at least today, maybe it wasn't
available at the time, but many exit, and then they do something else.
Was there a moment where you considered that, or what kept you from selling the company
when you grew from, say, 25 million to 100 million or something like this?
I think the proper answer is an annual analysis of what we're about from the point of view
of where the business was.
So every summer during holiday, there was, for my part anyway, always a reconsidering, is
this something I rather would not do and jump on something else?
And after a couple of weeks, pondering and thinking and trying to make an analyze the
situation I came always back with my best options to have an interesting future is to keep
stick with the business.
Well it was good that you did and that you didn't sell out because you managed to scale
this business and build a billion dollar plus company.
How was this possible this journey of growing first organically?
Lots of the times it's just stroke of luck, something happens and it's a good thing.
A lot of things that happens are not good things, but when good things happen, you can
profit from them and realize that you have had a turn of luck.
I mean, one early, not incident, but the event was we didn't have that much money.
So in the late 80s, graphic user interfaces were coming along.
The first, it was called MSDOS for old people, they know what it is.
It was an operating system for the PCs.
The big thing was IBM's OS2 as an operating system and to jump on a new technological platform.
We didn't have money to buy that development kit.
It was much cheaper to go with Microsoft and with Excel and the Windows development.
So that's why we chose that way in the next generation or software and we came out
several years ahead of competition.
That's just pure chance or maybe scarce resources that at that point put us on the proper place.
Another happy or lucky coincidence which was actually quite unlucky, we made an IPO in 98,
the first equity we raised really, in order to expand our business to Germany.
We went to Germany and within six months we realized we're only going to spend all those money
and not make any return.
Coming back to the board and saying it's not going to work and they said,
okay, you have promised now three thousand shareholders that you're going to conquer Germany,
you need to have a plan B which we didn't.
But that led us into the track of acquiring since we had the money
and we had sort of partners which was also very specialized providing software
for the proper management sector.
So picking up the phone and saying, should we meet, maybe we could coexist
and we have money and you have stuff.
So we made the first acquisition, proper acquisition in 98.
And then we made a number of those quadrupling the size of the company in 18 months
which brought havoc of course to the organization.
But further on a couple of years everything was in order and we realized that, okay,
that's one possible line of action trying to find other very specialized software companies
which at that point in time was not very much in demand.
Now were there any others that you saw who also were acquiring these type of businesses?
No, no.
Did you?
No, people were questioning what we were doing.
Everyone from the board, from the bank to the board to people around.
When was the first time you saw someone else doing the same as you were doing?
Because now it's more popular.
I heard of a constellation software maybe around 2010.
I'm not sure when but it was several, several years later.
We were absolutely sure we were the only one in the universe doing this kind of stuff.
And for those who don't know constellation software is a Canadian company.
What do you think of their journey compared to the one that you have done?
Well we started with nothing and they started with the street load of money.
That's the difference.
And you have both been successful in your own ways.
And they are much, much bigger.
Yes.
As of now.
When it comes to these type of businesses software you came in with like programming and these interesting computers,
many investors looking at these type of businesses today.
They really value the stability, the predictability of these revenues.
This was not really common at the time but you were very early,
one of the first probably who started with what is now called software as a service.
How did that happen?
The traditional model is license and maintenance fees.
Which we with success had done business within the property management.
But trying to use the traditional model when we were dealing with utility.
There were fewer maybe instead of a thousand possible customers since we had 60.
So we thought we needed to hike the license price, which was impossible.
It was now everywhere.
Then we came back one day and said I think we should sell this as a like a newspaper, like a subscription.
So they pay per month instead of this licensing model.
And we provided some extra services bundled in with the software.
And for the sake of the argument we tried to charge about 10,000 euros for the license,
which was a big no-no.
And then we came back and said you can have this as a subscription.
And it cost about 10,000 euros per year.
Oh, fine.
And I know it has to do with buying something is investment.
And that will trickle up the common chain.
And if it's only a subscription or an OPEX, someone else is making the decision.
You've been very successful acquiring businesses with that and also doing that in your own business since 1995 then when you started.
What are your thoughts now on this like fluctuations in your earnings?
How you keep a stability in that over the years?
Since a couple of years back we have acquired companies that has a more transactional based business model for reasons that are not possible to object to.
So you have to go with the flow.
And that means that there can be a bigger volatility in earnings.
In the long run it will even out.
And there are some sometimes these kind of companies when they try to find their business model includes a transactional items.
We have it in other parts also, but it's to much less extent than it has been what the last three or four years.
And if you look at the longer term, you've definitely been able to grow VTech very successfully in many dimensions.
Speaking about growth, I'm curious how do you measure whether you are successful in what you're doing?
Well, we have a few KPIs and the first hurdle to reach is when you're recurring revenue will cover your labor cost.
Then you know, any new sales you do will possibly hit the bottom line or a big chunk of it will hit the bottom line.
And then there is a constraint also when you reach more or less 100% recurring revenue, which is too complicated to.
It's easy on paper, it's more complicated to say it.
And the other one that I'm really interested in is comparing added value to labor cost.
Since we don't have any inventory and so forth, it's just some 75 to 80% of our cost base is our employees.
So tracking the rest is okay, could be interesting, but really you need to keep track of efficiency.
And that we are always improving within our own operation, that's key.
And if you are successful in doing that, we will improve our profitability and our cash flow, which we then can invest for future growth, both in our own software.
But hopefully a couple of acquisitions also.
You mentioned the people in your company, and that's an important aspect, of course.
And this book is a good testament to that, I think, as well. How do you motivate the right people to work for VTEC?
I think I wouldn't answer that question the way you put it.
I think people need to be motivated by their actual job description.
I can't motivate people to do a good work.
If the people working in our company is not motivated in doing a good job for the customer, for the sales or for the co-workers, you're lost.
So motivation has to come from inside. And of course, the job is then possibly to enable a culture and a place and a mission that attracts enough people in order for them to find it interesting and rewarding to work in our company.
I like that.
And when it comes to the growth, you have become a larger organization. You're still not a huge organization.
But how do you work to avoid unnecessary bureaucracy creeping into the administration and the organization?
To keep more or less all decisions in the business units.
And the overhead we are carrying today is IT because all those small verticals we have, they're doing an extremely good job.
But when it comes especially to IT security, you need to have some extra resources and muscles in order to stay on top of things.
And so a two a great extent that can be provide from the group level than as an internal consultants or maybe control part of our organization.
We have a very small HR department which are used by the business units on demand.
So it's just provided for internal services. And since they are internal also they know pretty much all about our culture and so forth.
And that can be in play very early on in especially recruitment processes.
And acquisitions is a big part of what you're doing and a way to grow. Can you say a bit more about how you're working with M&A?
We have a small group of people, depending on how you count through your form maybe, that is working full time.
And today is a lot of incoming. So I know last year we have looked at approximately 300 targets, more deeper analysis of about 200 made non-binding offer for 35 and close to 7 deals.
So it's a lot of work.
And the funding of these acquisitions is both with your cash flow that you generate from the businesses. It's also from leverage.
But you also have raised some capital historically. You are one of the larger shareholders. What are your thoughts on raising additional equity?
I think being a bit opportunistic and sometimes if you make the math it can actually be cheaper to have equity than to have going into that.
There are some boundaries that has to be fulfilled in order for that to work but at a particular point in time that can make sense.
The ultimate goal anyway is of course should be I think to be able to grow from your own cash flow which can be a bit demanding in software since investors value the recurring income stream very highly.
So if you are a series of acquiring industries they will go with a lower multiple because of the volatility in that business.
And has this changed over time?
25 years ago these kind of software companies were not very attractive. So multiples pass increased over time as the popularity has increased.
But still there's hardly rates you cannot. There is a limit what you can pay if you are an eternal owner and not someone who is buying for later sale of.
It seems like you have still been able to do a lot of acquisitions in recent years if we look out 10-20 years what do you foresee there?
There's a lot of companies and a lot of these highly specialized companies. And you I still get surprised actually of the incoming memorandums.
Yeah of course there has to be software that sector also. So there is a long run way.
We haven't spoken so much about geographies here where do you see that grow from where you are now?
I think we started out in Sweden in the north of Sweden and then sequentially went into Norway in Denmark and established fairly firm Nordic footprint.
So the first acquisition outside of the Nordic came in the Netherlands and then in Belgium. And I think Europe as a whole is a lot bigger than the Nordics.
And what we're doing here in the Nordics is I think we are front runners also.
Do you have any other lessons from the first 40 years of building Vitek that you would like to mention here that we haven't talked about?
Well that's the long list of mistakes.
Or maybe one example of putting your foot in the wrong direction or in the wrong spot.
Now one thing we did early on we had made this first acquisition of a company providing more or less invoicing for property management.
And then a couple of years later we bought a similar company in the southern part of Sweden and they were kind of head on the competition.
So we had two systems making more or less the same job and everybody was asking me and all of coworkers, the board, customers and others hanging around which system are you going to choose?
Because if you have two factories you will close down one in order to increase your usability of the one factory.
Eventually we caved to this and said we will go with this software and the other version and the customers from that company we lost about 50% of those customers over a period of five years and then we made an acquisition and bought them back.
And the lesson from that is you can't kill off a software unless you have made a transition that is more or less seamless for your customers and that will take some time.
But eventually that will pay off. So if we take the property management business in Sweden which we made six or seven acquisitions early on and they were hovering around the 5% margin for many years and we needed those license steals in order to make any profit at all.
It is way higher today and now we have one software suite. But it took us 15 years in making experiments and so forth. I think we can do it quickly today but not within the year and not within three years it will take more.
But we know how to do it. So that was a big mistake which maybe it could have been a real real crisis.
And another mistake which I actually I knew it was a mistake when we made it. We had within the real estate agents in Sweden there were two competing companies and they were fully functional both of those options so the only way they could compete was with pricing. It's a lousy situation.
In a way we had bought one of those companies and low and behold six months later the owner of the other company said we should cooperate which of course they wanted to sell their company to us and I said it's a monopoly situation that is not a good way to go.
Maybe we could make something from that. But of course an monopoly is never liked by the market so the real estate agents federation said we can't have this situation we need to develop our own software so the competition came back.
Fortunately for us was that the company we bought had two other software solutions for other markets and one of those was really really a golden egg which we found out afterwards so we made a huge mistake knowingly which we sort of mitigated over time and then within the package we had a really really nice operation.
It's fascinating to hear how things have been evolving and all those people you meet throughout the years and all the advice you get.
People have so many opinions as you alluded to there. Maybe you mentioned it already but if not what's the worst advice you ever got.
You can't be this diversified.
Who said that? You can't do software for utilities and the same time do software for property management.
There's so different you can't make this work and well we looked at the numbers and so we were profitable so obviously it worked.
So we disregard all those good advice.
It's good that you did and let's come back a bit more to the present time and she focused to where we are now after 35 years as CEO you left a position in 2021.
How has this transition been for you?
Personally well I spent sort of 10 years trying to mold the organization in order for me to step down.
So the transition has been extremely smooth for me and I have a really good cooperation with older who is the CEO now and I also have access to internal systems so I can do my own homework if I want to.
I don't need to bother people if I get curious.
The only big thing is that I don't have to be at the office all the time.
Otherwise I spend my time once again being curious and reading a lot of stuff and trying to stay on top of things and sometimes people ask me how I know this and that and I say I make it my business to know stuff.
How did you select your successor?
I've known only for 20 years or more and he was having really demanding positions during his career.
I've seen what he's done and what kind of operations he's been involved with and there was a small opportunity in time when he was available.
So I put the question if it was interested to come into the company as a CFO at that point.
We haven't worked together really. We have been on the same board for a number of years in the local company but otherwise it's more like how we're doing and so forth.
So we had a period of approximately two and a half years and then I was ripe to put the question.
And in the boardwork as a chairman, how do you avoid group thinking?
Now I think that has to do with the composition of the board and the board members.
It's a board we have assembled over a long period of time with different experiences from different industries and there's no hesitation to
to questions, suggestions that come along and that was the case also when I was the CEO.
So I think it's, it sorts itself out because of the people who are in the board and stuff get questioned and things sometimes stops in the board.
Not when it's presented as for a decision but earlier on we have sort of a process that discussions are coming along pretty early when new ideas or whatever is on the table.
So the board can have their feedback or make their feedback.
So when things don't evolve into actual things happening, it has probably gone away during those discussions.
So the board is very much not sitting as the final place for decisions to be made but is involved previously also in important aspects of the business development or business strategy maybe I should say.
And that's a discussion that is present on every board meeting. It's not something we discuss once a year, it's on every board meeting.
And besides being the chair of Vitech, what other commitments do you have in life?
I have three or four other boards. I have a chair of two others sitting on the fourth board also.
So it's that kind of activities I pursue. What type of companies and where are they based?
One, it's up north, it's close to family, close to home. One company is the holding company who is a subsidiary to the university which is actually doing seed investments in early startups deep tech emanating from.
Research and the system for fostering innovations and trying to make real businesses and not just fantastic ideas.
And the other one is a small family, more or less family owned investment company making not many investment but have made a substantial investment in a company that it's actually run by my brother which is sort of a local serial acquire but in the industry sector.
You're starting out or ten years down the line but still early stages.
Everything is about the perspective. It's clear from reading the book that Umiho has been very important for Vitech and Vitech has been very important for Umiho as a city.
This local presence, how is that these days in Vitech and also for Umiho?
As we have grown when we need people for senior positions within the group level, if we choose to make that kind of recruitment in Umiho, we get the look at them, we get the best the city can provide, the time can provide.
There is another aspect, I'm stubborn. Why is it not possible for us to have HQ in Umiho?
No, I think it's a good place to be. And it's a university town, you need to keep that in mind.
The university is very present within the city. For one thing, people having studied at the university are still working within the city.
And I think the statistics is that the level of education level of people living in Umiho is if not number one but number two in Sweden.
So there's a lot of both smart and educated people and maybe that's an environment I like.
And you being there is probably one reason for many people staying there as well, working for you and others in the ecosystem there.
When it comes to the local community, is there something else that Vitech has a company or you personally are doing to help the community?
Well, there is some payback, of course, and advisory boards and presentations maybe.
I'm going on a trip to Italy soon where I'm going to have a keynote speech for, I'm not sure, maybe 50, 60 entrepreneurs from Nordic, not counties,
but regions. So it's payback for more or less in that respect.
We're not putting a lot of money into sports or whatever, but students doing their final paper.
Speaking about sports, I know you also play some golf, which is both a physical and a mental game, has playing golf in any way influenced how you run Vitech.
I hope not.
Because golf is usually a very individual sport, but it can also be very social.
In the book, we learned that you play golf with all of your first business partner and the co-founder.
We haven't talked so much about him, how much do you talk with him these days and how is that relationship?
Nowadays it's a few and four between our talks, but going back in time, I mean, we spent hours per day discussing whatever and trying out ideas and comparing facts and views and stuff and so forth.
And then once in a while you need just to let the steam off and then there's goods to have someone that you are actually so closely connected to that we've been over the years.
We spent a lot of time together and nowadays it's not so necessary. We have other people running the business better than we ever did.
But both of you have remained large shareholders of Vitech. Have you done any other investments yourself or with him?
We haven't done anything together and I've made some small failed attempts.
It's probably been a wise decision to keep most of the money in the business.
You have been growing that pile at a good clip over the last decades. How has that impact you to get at least on paper a lot of money?
I have a car I only use during summer. I can take off the roof.
And then people say why do you have a convertible up where you live? That's where we live. That's actually the place to have it. You don't take down the roof every day.
So otherwise not to a great extent.
And in the beginning you bought those, you could buy those technical stuff, those computers with the money you earned.
But maybe that came to a halt at some point. You had enough to buy what you wanted to have.
Well from computers and stuff, yeah sure. And I'm not really that excited anymore to get the latest equipment. I tend to stick with what works nowadays.
So now I'm not buying a lot of things.
And speaking about technology, it's been so many shifts and you've seen this firsthand how technology has changed and you mentioned windows there as one example.
And also many technologies of course that someone believed it and they didn't play out as expected.
What have you learned from this when we look at what companies make and the mistakes they make when they are these kind of technology shifts?
Well there is a very wise saying that you overestimate the impact of new technology in the short term and underestimate it in the long term.
Which means when new stuff comes along you have time.
I think that's the takeaway from that statement which I find is actually true.
So new technology will eventually be very very important but you don't have to rush into it in order to use it in the most efficient way.
So there is one saying that we have borrowed from somewhere that says we should be on the leading edge of technology not the leading edge of technology.
So you need to know what's happening and have a decent grasp of what's happening.
But I think having a more long term view of technology and technology changes means that you can jump on the wagon in the right time when it's mature to the extent that you can actually make good use of it.
Then it seems like the cycle may be have shortened with AI.
There are things that you can put in practice fairly quick.
And I'm not talking about coding because that is an evolution from when you had to do everything yourself.

thesis: The podcast features Lars Stenlund, chairman of Vitek Software, discussing his book 'Driven by Curiosity,' which documents the company's 40-year journey from a small venture at Umeå University to a leading provider of vertical software solutions.
